To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cytosolic Prion protein (PrPC) has a neuroprotective function that is cell type-specific.
the untranslocated form PrP is neuroprotective in a cell type-dependent manner.

1) untranslocated PrPC can be found in neurons, 2) untranslocated prion protein protects neurons against cell death, 3) the neuroprotective effect of untranslocated prions is cell type specific and 4) the mechanism by which untranslocated prP exerts its neuroprotective activity is still unclear and needs to be further studied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cytosolic prion protein in neuronal viability and its possible implications in prion diseases and in other neurodegenerative diseases.
the role of the prion in neurodegenerative diseases, in particular the prion's role as an anti-apoptotic protein in the brain.
a better understanding of the mechanisms of PrP translocon-mediated transport and the physiological role of cytosolic untranslocated PrPC in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cytosolic prion protein is a neuroprotective factor in cortical and hippocampus neurons, but not in granules neurons.

the untranslocated cytosolic form is a physiological form of PrP that can be found in neurons, that it is neuroprotective in some brain regions but not in others, and that its synthesis and accumulation is controlled by a mechanism that involves the proteasome.
PrPC can be translocated to the cytosolic compartment in some neurons and that the presence of this form of PrP in neurons can protect them against apoptotic stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
untranslocated cytosolic PrPC has a protective function against apoptotic insults in neurons, and that this protective function is cell-type-specific.
the untranslocated form, but not the translocated form, of PrP is neuroprotective.

the PrP signal peptide is a key element for the correct translocation of PrP to the ER lumen, and that the untranslocated PrPC is a neuroprotective factor in cortical and hippocampus neurons, but not in granule neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PrP can exert a cytoprotective effect in neurons.
the cytosolic PrPC can be generated by two distinct mechanisms, and the resulting PrPC can be either toxic or neuroprotective depending on cell type and context.
the cytosolic form might serve as a neuroprotective factor in the central nervous system, and that the efficiency of Prion Protein (PrP) translocation might be a cell-type-specific process.
